title: Methods in Context: Choosing Methods for Education
welcome_lead: Questionnaires vs interviews in schools — choose carefully.

walkthroughs.body_html: Schools are busy, hierarchical and protected. Access often requires multiple gatekeepers — LA, head, parent, pupil. Pupils may seek peer approval over honesty. Power imbalance with adult researcher affects validity. Younger pupils have shorter attention spans.

The PERVERT framework asks: Practical (time, cost, access), Ethical (consent, harm), Reliability, Validity, Examples (specific to topic), Researcher (skills, gender, ethnicity), Theoretical (positivism vs interpretivism). Apply each strand to chosen method.

Questionnaires: fast, large samples, low validity with younger children. Structured interviews: standardised but intimidating. Participant observation: rich but raises ethics. Official statistics: free but defined by state. Choice depends on topic — pupil identities suit qualitative; achievement gaps suit quantitative.

Why do positivists and interpretivists prefer different methods?
options: Positivists like numbers and interpretivists like words — that's the whole difference.

Positivists treat sociology like natural science, seeking objective measurable patterns — preferring quantitative methods. Interpretivists believe humans construct meaning, requiring qualitative methods to access subjective experience.
Both positivists and interpretivists prefer experiments above all else.

mcqs.q: Why do positivists prefer quantitative methods?
options: Because numbers are easier to collect than words.
They produce objective, reliable, generalisable data resembling natural science.
